parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”), from ἀφορίζω (aphorízō, “I define, mark off or determine”), from ἀπό (apó, “off”) + ὁρίζω (horízō, “I divide, bound”), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
Ultimately from Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”).

parole.significato: psychology (the science of human behavior and the human mind)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”), with the suffix -ia (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: toxic, poisonous (having harmful effects on the organism)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin toxicus (“poisoned”), from Latin toxicum (“poison”), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón) φάρμακον (phármakon, “poison for use on arrows”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).

Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
